aiMachineReadReview.question: Starting from the machine index, how do I install the public Python package and create my first persistent APKG?
aiMachineReadReview.answer: Create a virtual environment with `python -m venv .venv`, activate it with `. .venv/bin/activate`, then run `python -m pip install ankiforge==0.3.1`. On Windows use `.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1`. Use ordinary CPython 3.11+ and a matching platform wheel; the recorded release checks cover 3.11–3.14. The linked quickstart constructs `Project('spanish', default_deck='Spanish')`, adds key `es:hola` with `Note.basic('hola', 'hello')`, and calls `project.build(BuildOptions.to('spanish.apkg'))`. Running `python main.py` writes a persistent Spanish deck. Keep the namespace and note key stable; export itself does not require Anki. [Python quickstart](https://ankiforge.dev/docs/python-quickstart/index.md); installation and runtime are also visible directly in [the index](https://ankiforge.dev/llms.txt). This is a reading-based answer, not a newly executed installation.
conclusions: Public package and version are directly discoverable without source checkout.
The exported Markdown preserves the runnable install block, complete minimum program, persistence and identity conditions.

aiMachineReadReview.question: Where is the Node API, and how do authoring, asynchronous build/compare, reports and artifact ownership work?
aiMachineReadReview.answer: The index's API references link directly to the Node and TypeScript API. Author with `new Project(namespace)`, `.defaultDeck(name)`, `.add(key, note)`, `Note.basic`/`Note.cloze`, and immutable custom models. `await project.build(BuildOptions.to(path))` returns BuildOutput with an owning artifact; `await project.compare(CompareOptions.against(path))` returns a ComparisonReport even when policy blocks publication. `BuildReport` is observations, not outcome or file ownership; snapshots use snake_case JSON names. Media reads and build/compare are asynchronous, and build/compare use a captured project snapshot. Retain an artifact owner while reading its path; the last temporary owner removes the file, whereas a persistent file survives close. `preparePublication` permits review before publish, and each `publish()` attempt consumes the prepared owner. [Node API](https://ankiforge.dev/docs/node-api/index.md), discovered through [the index](https://ankiforge.dev/llms.txt). I did not execute these APIs in this reading task.
conclusions: Tables, complete code blocks, report/null distinctions and ownership limitations remain readable in Markdown.
Public 0.3.1 prepared-publication availability is stated locally and distinguished from lifecycle guarantees.

aiMachineReadReview.question: Can I build a deck from JSON with media, then review an answer-only update, and what is the valid baseline?
aiMachineReadReview.answer: Use the JSON task guide linked by the index. Download v1.json, v2.json, cell.png and tone.wav into `recipe/`, then choose its complete Rust, Python or Node/TypeScript program for public Anki Forge 0.3.1. The caller parses JSON; each release is expected to contain 3 notes, 3 cards and 2 media files. v2 changes only the first answer. The program creates original `v1.apkg`, compares the next project against it, saves `comparison.json`, prepares `v2.apkg` with that baseline, saves `review.json`, checks policy again, then publishes. Expected evidence is `RISK.NOTE_CHANGED`, no added/removed notes, and publication allowed for this edit. Preserve namespace `biology-json`, durable note IDs and the original distribution v1 APKG. An Anki re-export is not a valid substitute. Importing does not delete omitted notes, and client settings/local changes can affect outcomes. [JSON guide](https://ankiforge.dev/docs/json-to-anki/index.md), found in [the index](https://ankiforge.dev/llms.txt). These are documented expectations, not new SDK execution results.
conclusions: All three SDK sections survive export, including commands, code, shared attachments and expected results.
Original-baseline, policy-review and Anki-client restrictions are preserved near the update instructions.

aiMachineReadReview.question: What package/runtime/platform scope is documented, and what does a successful export not guarantee about Anki clients or updates?
aiMachineReadReview.answer: The compatibility guide identifies public Rust/npm/PyPI 0.3.1 packages, with its stated 2026-10-13 check date. It records Rust 1.92/current stable, Node 22.13/current 22/24/26, and ordinary CPython 3.11–3.14 checks. Native package platforms are macOS arm64/x64, Linux x64 GNU/glibc and Windows x64. Package availability is not proof for every host. Browser, Electron, Bun, Alpine/musl and ARM64 Linux/Windows are outside recorded Node scope; other Python implementations, free-threaded interpreters and subinterpreters require separate validation. Export needs no Anki, but import/render/playback depend on client version, codecs and settings. The guide explicitly limits the cited 40 benchmark checks and requires original distribution APKGs for updates; re-exports lose needed identity evidence, and omissions do not delete learner notes. [Compatibility](https://ankiforge.dev/docs/compatibility/index.md), found under Start here in [the index](https://ankiforge.dev/llms.txt). I have read these scope statements; I have not rerun the linked release or GUI checks.
conclusions: Runtime/platform table and dated verification scope are readable without following external sources.
Index summary and detailed guide agree on export independence, valid update baseline and client limitations.
